Time Expressions with the Present Perfect

You can use time expressions with the Present Perfect or with the Past Simple. The Past Simple refers to completed, specific time like “yesterday” or “in 1973.” Other time expressions may be used with either the Past Simple or the Present Perfect.

When you are reading, you don't need to understand every single word. You can just concentrate on the important words, and the others will be obvious based on the context of the text.
Generally, you need to be able to identify most of the shorter words in a text. These are usually the most important words.
Negative words, such as neither, never and nobody.
Nobody has ever climbed to the top.
Prepositions, such as in, on, at or under.
The mouse was hiding under the table.
Conjunctions, such as for, nor, but and yet.
He had eaten a great deal, yet he was still hungry.
And finally, question words, such as who, what, when, which and where.
Words from this final group can act as relative pronouns at the beginning of relative clauses.
My brother, who won the science award three years ago, built his own hot air balloon.
What I really want is to go to the park.
The chair which was broken has been taken to the dump.
We can do whatever he wants to do.

images.text:
Avalanches, hurricanes, and earthquakes are just some of the ways that the earth reminds us who is in control. No matter how much we humans think we can control nature, nature always manages to surprise us. All my life, I've heard incredible stories about natural disasters.
Since I was a child, I've had a fascination with hurricanes, which are incredibly strong windstorms that usually start over the ocean and strike coastal cities. The winds are so strong that often homes are destroyed and people are injured or killed. The only protection against a hurricane may be to evacuate the area. A close friend of mine was in New Orleans in 2005 when Katrina hit. She was lucky to escape before being trapped by floods and has recently become a volunteer for a disaster relief organization because of her experience.

It is also difficult to protect yourself against earthquakes, which are so dangerous that it is not uncommon for homes to collapse and bury people. Rescue teams in earthquake-prone areas rescue people and save lives, but their job is challenging. My uncle who moved to Nepal before the earthquake wreaked havoc there, rescued a few people from disaster.
Of all the natural disasters I've heard about, it's avalanches that frighten me the most. Although avalanches are less common events, they still pose a serious threat to property and human lives. Avalanches are unforeseeable events which can throw a person down a mountain slope with no control.

For decades, my brother has snowboarded on mountain ranges around the world. He has recently been to the Rocky Mountains in British Columbia, Canada where he watched an avalanche roll down a mountain. His friend John, who was with him, was once trapped in an avalanche. Before he was buried, he remembered to cover his face with his arm to create an air pocket. Fortunately, because he did that he survived.
Natural disasters come from the sky, the sea or from inside the earth. No matter what the source, all natural disasters share power, strength and the potential to cause serious damage.

contents.value: Avalanches are just one of the ways that nature has to remind us about the need to take care of the environment. Of all the natural disasters that affect people who live in the mountains, avalanches tend to be the most common, yet nobody works consistently to reduce their impact. Whatever action is taken to prevent avalanches, local communities must be involved.
